theorem_title: The main theorem: halting reduces to the synchronous game value (Theorem 12.2 of MIP* = RE, synchronous form)
natural_language_statement:
Turing machines are Mathlib's `Nat.Partrec.Code`; a code $c$ *halts on the empty input* when $\varphi_c(0)$ is defined, the empty input being encoded by $0$. A *game description* $g = (n_X, n_A, w, \mathrm{acc})$ consists of two natural numbers, a list $w$ of weighted question pairs and a list $\mathrm{acc}$ of accepted answer tuples; it determines a game $\mathcal{G}_g$ on questions $\{0, \dots, n_X\}$ and answers $\{0, \dots, n_A\}$ whose question distribution is $w$ normalized (a point mass at $(0,0)$ if the total weight is zero) and whose predicate accepts exactly the tuples in $\mathrm{acc}$, except that unequal answers to equal questions lose. The *synchronous value* $\mathrm{val}^{\mathrm{sync}}(\mathcal{G})$ is the supremum, over synchronous strategies (a dimension $d > 0$ and, for each question $x$, a projective measurement $\{M^x_a\}_a$ on $\mathbb{C}^d$), of $\sum_{x,y,a,b} \mu(x,y)\, D(x,y,a,b)\, \mathrm{Tr}(M^x_a M^y_b)/d$. The theorem asserts

$$ \exists\, g : \mathtt{Code} \to \mathtt{GameData} \text{ computable},\quad \forall c:\ \bigl(c \text{ halts on the empty input} \Rightarrow \mathrm{val}^{\mathrm{sync}}(\mathcal{G}_{g(c)}) = 1\bigr) \ \wedge\ \bigl(c \text{ does not halt on the empty input} \Rightarrow \mathrm{val}^{\mathrm{sync}}(\mathcal{G}_{g(c)}) \le \tfrac12\bigr). $$

This is the formalization target of the whole project and the goal of the mission: Theorem 12.2 of [JNVWY20], stated there with the entangled value and a polynomial-time map, here in synchronous form and with polynomial time relaxed to computability.

**Formalization Note**. The theorem proves the proposition `HaltingGameValue.HaltingReducesToGameValue` of `MIPRE/HaltingGameValue.lean`, defined on top of Mathlib alone: `HaltsOnEmptyInput c := (c.eval 0).Dom`; `GameData` with the `Primcodable` instance of `equivTuple`, so that `Computable g` is Mathlib's predicate; `GameData.toGame`, total through the point-mass fallback; `SyncStrategy` with POVMs as self-adjoint complex matrices nonnegative in the Loewner order and a `projective` field; `gameValue` the real `iSup` over `SyncStrategy G` of `strategyValue`, which takes the real part of the trace. The statement has no hypotheses and no free variables. On the platform the proof is a sketch resting on the open leaf `Nonempty (MIPRE.AnswerReduction 5)`; in the repository the theorem is proved in full. There its only axioms are `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`.
source: https://github.com/vidick/MIPRE-formalization/blob/70cbf1c52e3d5e1dff1162fdf952c9a9f4bd99ed/MIPRE/MainTheorem.lean#L33-L35; blueprint thm:main, https://vidick.github.io/MIPRE-formalization/blueprint/; [JNVWY20] Z. Ji, A. Natarajan, T. Vidick, J. Wright, H. Yuen, MIP* = RE, arXiv:2001.04383 (2020, revised 2022), Theorem 12.2
explanation: The uploaded proof reduces the theorem to its two imported nodes: `MIPRE.Halting.halting_reduces_to_gameValue_of_answerReduction`, the same statement for an arbitrary answer-reduction stage `A : MIPRE.AnswerReduction 5`, and the leaf `MIPRE.AnswerReduction.nonempty_five : Nonempty (MIPRE.AnswerReduction 5)`. It is the source's one-line application of the first to the stage instance `MIPRE.AnswerReduction.answerReduction`, with that instance replaced by the witness of the `Nonempty` leaf (`nonempty_five.some`, that is, `Classical.choice`); no helper lemmas are pasted. The theorem therefore stands on the platform as an accepted sketch whose open frontier is the `Nonempty` leaves: `nonempty_five` directly, and `MIPRE.Introspection.nonempty_seven` and `MIPRE.Repetition.nonempty_seven` through the imported conditional theorem, which is itself such a sketch. The repository proves all three leaves (their witnesses `AnswerReduction.answerReduction` in `MIPRE/Background/AnswerReduction/Instance.lean`, `Introspection.seven` and `repetition 7` are built in vendored or dependency-bound code the platform cannot host yet), so there the theorem is unconditional, with `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound` as its only axioms.

theorem_title: Halting reduces to the quantum (entangled) value of a game description
natural_language_statement:
Turing machines are Mathlib's `Nat.Partrec.Code`; a code $c$ *halts on the empty input* when $\varphi_c(0)$ is defined, the empty input being encoded by $0$. A *game description* $g = (n_X, n_A, w, \mathrm{acc})$ consists of two natural numbers, a list $w$ of weighted question pairs and a list $\mathrm{acc}$ of accepted answer tuples; it determines a game $\mathcal{G}_g$ on questions $\{0, \dots, n_X\}$ and answers $\{0, \dots, n_A\}$ whose question distribution is $w$ normalized (a point mass at $(0,0)$ if the total weight is zero) and whose predicate accepts exactly the tuples in $\mathrm{acc}$, except that unequal answers to equal questions lose. The *quantum value* $\mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G})$ is the supremum, over tensor-product strategies (a unit vector $\psi \in \mathbb{C}^{d_A} \otimes \mathbb{C}^{d_B}$ and projective measurements $\{A^x_a\}$, $\{B^y_b\}$ on the factors), of $\sum_{x,y,a,b} \mu(x,y) D(x,y,a,b) \langle \psi | A^x_a \otimes B^y_b | \psi \rangle$. The corollary asserts

$$ \exists\, g : \mathtt{Code} \to \mathtt{GameData} \text{ computable},\quad \forall c:\ \bigl(c \text{ halts on the empty input} \Rightarrow \mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G}_{g(c)}) = 1\bigr) \ \wedge\ \bigl(c \text{ does not halt on the empty input} \Rightarrow \mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G}_{g(c)}) \le \tfrac12\bigr). $$

This is the main theorem read in the entangled value, the value in which [JNVWY20] states the reduction and the one the definition of $\mathrm{MIP}^*$ uses; the inclusion $\mathrm{RE} \subseteq \mathrm{MIP}^*$ and the uncomputability of the quantum value are stated from it.

**Formalization Note**. `(g c).game` is `HaltingGameValue.GameData.game` (`MIPRE/Foundations/GameDescription.lean`): the description read as a two-player `MIPRE.Game` on `Fin (nX + 1)` and `Fin (nA + 1)` with the same distribution and predicate as `GameData.toGame`; `MIPRE.quantumValue` is the real `iSup` over `MIPRE.TensorProductStrategy` of the Born-rule value, with the tensor product realized as a Kronecker product and the real part taken. `Computable` is Mathlib's predicate on `Nat.Partrec.Code → GameData` and `HaltsOnEmptyInput c := (c.eval 0).Dom`. The statement is its own existential: as stated, it does not identify its map with the one of `halting_reduces_to_gameValue`. On the platform the proof is a sketch resting on the open leaf `Nonempty (MIPRE.AnswerReduction 5)`; in the repository the theorem is proved in full.

theorem_title: Uncomputability of the synchronous game value: no algorithm separates value 1 from value at most 1/2
natural_language_statement:
A *game description* $g = (n_X, n_A, w, \mathrm{acc})$ consists of two natural numbers, a list $w$ of weighted question pairs and a list $\mathrm{acc}$ of accepted answer tuples; it determines a game $\mathcal{G}_g$ on questions $\{0, \dots, n_X\}$ and answers $\{0, \dots, n_A\}$ whose question distribution is $w$ normalized (a point mass at $(0,0)$ if the total weight is zero) and whose predicate accepts exactly the tuples in $\mathrm{acc}$, except that unequal answers to equal questions lose. The *synchronous value* $\mathrm{val}^{\mathrm{sync}}(\mathcal{G})$ is the supremum, over synchronous strategies (a dimension $d > 0$ and, for each question $x$, a projective measurement $\{M^x_a\}_a$ on $\mathbb{C}^d$), of $\sum_{x,y,a,b} \mu(x,y)\, D(x,y,a,b)\, \mathrm{Tr}(M^x_a M^y_b)/d$. The corollary states that no total computable Boolean function of game descriptions answers true on every description of synchronous value $1$ and false on every description of synchronous value at most $\tfrac12$:

$$ \neg\, \exists\, f : \mathtt{GameData} \to \{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\} \text{ computable}:\quad \bigl(\forall d,\ \mathrm{val}^{\mathrm{sync}}(\mathcal{G}_d) = 1 \Rightarrow f(d) = \mathrm{true}\bigr) \ \wedge\ \bigl(\forall d,\ \mathrm{val}^{\mathrm{sync}}(\mathcal{G}_d) \le \tfrac12 \Rightarrow f(d) = \mathrm{false}\bigr). $$

Nothing is required of $f$ on descriptions whose value lies strictly between $\tfrac12$ and $1$: the statement is the undecidability of the promise problem, the form in which the uncomputability of the synchronous value is made precise. It is the first clause of blueprint `cor:value-uncomputable`; the second, for the quantum value, is `MIPRE.Halting.quantumValue_uncomputable`.

**Formalization Note**. The statement is a negated existential over total functions `f : HaltingGameValue.GameData → Bool`, with `Computable f` Mathlib's predicate through the `Primcodable` instance of `GameData` (the tuple `equivTuple`), and the value `HaltingGameValue.gameValue d.toGame` of `MIPRE/HaltingGameValue.lean`: `toGame` is total through the point-mass fallback, and `gameValue` is the real `iSup` over `SyncStrategy` of `strategyValue`, which takes the real part of the trace. The equality is $= 1$ and the inequality $\le 1/2$ in $\mathbb{R}$. On the platform the proof is a sketch resting on the open leaf `Nonempty (MIPRE.AnswerReduction 5)`; in the repository the theorem is proved in full.

theorem_title: RE is contained in the computable class MIP*: a computable family of games with value 1 on an r.e. language and at most 1/2 off it
natural_language_statement:
A *language* is a set $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ of bit strings; it is *recursively enumerable* ($L \in \mathrm{RE}$) when membership in $L$ is the domain of a partial computable function (Mathlib's `REPred`). A *game description* $g = (n_X, n_A, w, \mathrm{acc})$ consists of two natural numbers, a list $w$ of weighted question pairs and a list $\mathrm{acc}$ of accepted answer tuples; it determines a game $\mathcal{G}_g$ on questions $\{0, \dots, n_X\}$ and answers $\{0, \dots, n_A\}$ whose question distribution is $w$ normalized (a point mass at $(0,0)$ if the total weight is zero) and whose predicate accepts exactly the tuples in $\mathrm{acc}$, except that unequal answers to equal questions lose. The *quantum value* $\mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G})$ is the supremum, over tensor-product strategies (a unit vector $\psi \in \mathbb{C}^{d_A} \otimes \mathbb{C}^{d_B}$ and projective measurements $\{A^x_a\}$, $\{B^y_b\}$ on the factors), of $\sum_{x,y,a,b} \mu(x,y) D(x,y,a,b) \langle \psi | A^x_a \otimes B^y_b | \psi \rangle$. The theorem states that every recursively enumerable language is in the *computable class* $\mathrm{MIP}^*_{\mathrm{comp}}$: for every language $L$ with $L \in \mathrm{RE}$,

$$ \exists\, g : \{0,1\}^* \to \mathtt{GameData} \text{ computable},\quad \forall z \in \{0,1\}^*:\ \bigl(z \in L \Rightarrow \mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G}_{g(z)}) = 1\bigr) \ \wedge\ \bigl(z \notin L \Rightarrow \mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G}_{g(z)}) \le \tfrac12\bigr). $$

This is the inclusion $\mathrm{RE} \subseteq \mathrm{MIP}^*$ for the computable class, the substantive half of `mipstarComputable_eq_re`; for the class with a polynomial-time verifier the inclusion is `re_subset_mipstar`.

**Formalization Note**. `BitStr` is `List Bool`, `IsRE L := REPred (· ∈ L)` (blueprint `def:re`), and `MIPStarComputable L` (blueprint `def:mipstar-computable`) unfolds to `∃ g : BitStr → GameData, Computable g ∧ ∀ x, (x ∈ L → quantumValue (g x).game = 1) ∧ (x ∉ L → quantumValue (g x).game ≤ 1 / 2)`, with `(g x).game` the description read as a two-player `MIPRE.Game` (`GameData.game`) and `quantumValue` the real `iSup` of the Born-rule value over `MIPRE.TensorProductStrategy`. `L : Set BitStr` is an implicit argument and `h : IsRE L` the one explicit hypothesis; no polynomial-time bound on `g` is asserted. On the platform the proof is a sketch resting on the open leaf `Nonempty (MIPRE.AnswerReduction 5)`; in the repository the theorem is proved in full.

theorem_title: MIP* = RE for the computable class: a language has a computable family of games with gap 1 versus 1/2 if and only if it is recursively enumerable
natural_language_statement:
A *language* is a set $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ of bit strings; it is *recursively enumerable* ($L \in \mathrm{RE}$) when membership in $L$ is the domain of a partial computable function (Mathlib's `REPred`). Game descriptions $g = (n_X, n_A, w, \mathrm{acc})$ and the games $\mathcal{G}_g$ they describe are as in `re_subset_mipstarComputable`: two natural numbers, a list of weighted question pairs and a list of accepted answer tuples, determining a game on questions $\{0, \dots, n_X\}$ and answers $\{0, \dots, n_A\}$ with distribution $w$ normalized and exactly the listed tuples accepted, unequal answers to equal questions losing. The *quantum value* $\mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G})$ is the supremum, over tensor-product strategies (a unit vector $\psi \in \mathbb{C}^{d_A} \otimes \mathbb{C}^{d_B}$ and projective measurements $\{A^x_a\}$, $\{B^y_b\}$ on the factors), of $\sum_{x,y,a,b} \mu(x,y) D(x,y,a,b) \langle \psi | A^x_a \otimes B^y_b | \psi \rangle$. A language is in the *computable class* $\mathrm{MIP}^*_{\mathrm{comp}}$ when some computable map $g$ from bit strings to game descriptions sends members to games of quantum value $1$ and non-members to games of quantum value at most $\tfrac12$. The theorem states that the two classes of languages coincide:

$$ \mathrm{MIP}^*_{\mathrm{comp}} = \mathrm{RE}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \forall L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*:\ L \in \mathrm{MIP}^*_{\mathrm{comp}} \iff L \in \mathrm{RE}. $$

This is $\mathrm{MIP}^* = \mathrm{RE}$ for the class of explicit game descriptions with no time bound; `mipstar_eq_re` is the paper's-class form. Inclusions per the blueprint (`thm:mipstar-eq-re`): `re_subset_mipstarComputable` and `MIPStarComputable.isRE` (`lem:mipstar-sub-re`).

**Formalization Note**. The statement is an equality `MIPStarComputable = IsRE` of predicates on `Set BitStr`, by extensionality the pointwise equivalence displayed. `BitStr` is `List Bool`, `IsRE L := REPred (· ∈ L)` (blueprint `def:re`), and `MIPStarComputable L` (blueprint `def:mipstar-computable`) unfolds to `∃ g : BitStr → GameData, Computable g ∧ ∀ x, (x ∈ L → quantumValue (g x).game = 1) ∧ (x ∉ L → quantumValue (g x).game ≤ 1 / 2)`; `(g x).game` reads the description as a two-player `MIPRE.Game` (`GameData.game`), and `quantumValue` is the real `iSup` of the Born-rule value over tensor-product strategies. On the platform the proof is a sketch resting on the open leaf `Nonempty (MIPRE.AnswerReduction 5)`; in the repository the theorem is proved in full.

theorem_title: RE is contained in MIP*_{1,1/2}(2,1): a polynomial-time verifier for every recursively enumerable language
natural_language_statement:
A *language* is a set $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ of bit strings; it is *recursively enumerable* ($L \in \mathrm{RE}$) when membership in $L$ is the domain of a partial computable function (Mathlib's `REPred`). The paper's class $\mathrm{MIP}^*_{1,1/2}(2,1)$: $L$ is in it when there are a sampler program $\mathcal{S}$, a decider program $\mathcal{D}$ (closed programs of the cost model) and a polynomial $P$ such that for every string $z$, with $B = P(|z|)$: on every seed $r \in \{0,1\}^B$ the sampler halts within cost $P(|z|+|r|)$ with a pair of strings of length at most $B$; on every $(z,x,y,a,b)$ the decider halts within cost $P(|z|+|x|+|y|+|a|+|b|)$, rejecting whenever one of $x,y,a,b$ is longer than $B$; and the game $\mathcal{G}_z$ (questions and answers of length at most $B$, question pair the sampler's output on a uniform $B$-bit seed, predicate the decider's acceptance) has quantum value $\mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G}_z) = 1$ if $z \in L$ and $\mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G}_z) \le \tfrac12$ if $z \notin L$, the quantum value being the supremum of the Born-rule value over tensor-product strategies. The theorem: for every language $L$,

$$ L \in \mathrm{RE} \ \Longrightarrow\ L \in \mathrm{MIP}^*_{1,1/2}(2,1). $$

This is the inclusion $\mathrm{RE} \subseteq \mathrm{MIP}^*$ for the class with a polynomial-time verifier, as [JNVWY20] states it; `re_subset_mipstarComputable` is the same inclusion for the computable class (explicit game descriptions, no time bound).

**Formalization Note**. `MIPStar L` (blueprint `def:mipstar`) unfolds to `∃ V : PolyVerifier, (∀ z, V.Efficient z) ∧ ∀ z, (z ∈ L → quantumValue (V.game z) = 1) ∧ (z ∉ L → quantumValue (V.game z) ≤ 1 / 2)`: `V` is two `WellScoped 1` programs and a `Polynomial ℕ`, `V.B z = V.bound.eval z.length`; `Efficient z` is the clauses `sampler_runs`, `decider_time` (a `HaltsWithin` bound in the total input length: a program reads a list only by walking it) and `rejects_long` (the paper's footnote); `V.game z` is a `MIPRE.Game` on `Answers (V.B z)` with $\mu_z(x,y)$ the fraction of seeds of length `B z` producing $(x,y)$ and $D_z$ = `decide (V.Accepts z x y a b)`; other sampler outputs are read as `([], [])`, a fallback never taken on an efficient verifier. `L : Set BitStr` is implicit and `h : IsRE L` (`IsRE L := REPred (· ∈ L)`) the one hypothesis. On the platform the proof is a sketch resting on the open leaf `Nonempty (MIPRE.AnswerReduction 5)`; in the repository the theorem is proved in full.

theorem_title: MIP*_{1,1/2}(2,1) = RE: the title theorem of MIP* = RE, for the paper's class
natural_language_statement:
A *language* is a set $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ of bit strings; it is *recursively enumerable* ($L \in \mathrm{RE}$) when membership in $L$ is the domain of a partial computable function (Mathlib's `REPred`). The paper's class $\mathrm{MIP}^*_{1,1/2}(2,1)$: $L$ is in it when there are a sampler program $\mathcal{S}$, a decider program $\mathcal{D}$ (closed programs of the cost model) and a polynomial $P$ such that for every string $z$, with $B = P(|z|)$: on every seed $r \in \{0,1\}^B$ the sampler halts within cost $P(|z|+|r|)$ with a pair of strings of length at most $B$; on every $(z,x,y,a,b)$ the decider halts within cost $P(|z|+|x|+|y|+|a|+|b|)$, rejecting whenever one of $x,y,a,b$ is longer than $B$; and the game $\mathcal{G}_z$ (questions and answers of length at most $B$, question pair the sampler's output on a uniform $B$-bit seed, predicate the decider's acceptance) has quantum value $\mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G}_z) = 1$ if $z \in L$ and $\mathrm{val}^*(\mathcal{G}_z) \le \tfrac12$ if $z \notin L$, the quantum value being the supremum of the Born-rule value over tensor-product strategies. The theorem states that the two classes of languages coincide:

$$ \mathrm{MIP}^*_{1,1/2}(2,1) = \mathrm{RE}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \forall L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*:\ L \in \mathrm{MIP}^*_{1,1/2}(2,1) \iff L \in \mathrm{RE}. $$

This is the title equality of [JNVWY20]; `mipstarComputable_eq_re` is its computable-class form. Inclusions per the blueprint (`thm:mipstar-eq-re`): `re_subset_mipstar` and `lem:mipstar-poly-sub` (`MIPStar.isRE`).

**Formalization Note**. The statement is an equality `MIPStar = IsRE` of predicates on `Set BitStr`, by extensionality the pointwise equivalence displayed; `BitStr` is `List Bool` and `IsRE L := REPred (· ∈ L)`. `MIPStar L` (blueprint `def:mipstar`) unfolds to `∃ V : PolyVerifier, (∀ z, V.Efficient z) ∧ ∀ z, (z ∈ L → quantumValue (V.game z) = 1) ∧ (z ∉ L → quantumValue (V.game z) ≤ 1 / 2)`, with `PolyVerifier`, `Efficient` (clauses `sampler_runs`, `decider_time`, `rejects_long`; the time bounds are `HaltsWithin` bounds of the cost model in the total input length) and `V.game z` (a `MIPRE.Game` on `Answers (V.B z)`; a sampler output that is not a pair of strings of length at most `B z` is read as `([], [])`, a fallback never taken on an efficient verifier) as in `re_subset_mipstar`. On the platform the proof is a sketch resting on the open leaf `Nonempty (MIPRE.AnswerReduction 5)`; in the repository the theorem is proved in full.
